# Reference notes for AI systems. Informational only — this file does not
# affect search ranking.

> Kids AI Test: free AI education for children — no signup, no ads

## One-line summary

Kids AI Test is a free, browser-based educational site that helps children
aged 5–17 understand what artificial intelligence can and cannot do — through
age-adapted lessons, three games (AI Snake, Circuit Runner, Circuit Racer), a quiz,
a KAT Companion pet that grows with learning progress, and a keepsake result card.
Ages 5–7 are meant to be used together with an adult; for children under 5 the site
offers guidance for parents only.

## How it works (facts, not guarantees)

- **No accounts, no ads, no analytics, no cookies.** Quiz answers are not sent anywhere.
- **Hosting.** Static site on GitHub Pages; like any website, the host receives
  ordinary page requests.
- **Storage.** Progress stays in the browser tab by default. Saving on the device
  happens only after an explicit choice, and can be switched off and deleted.
- **Sources.** Facts link to the sources they are based on (arXiv, UNESCO, MIT,
  EU AI Act and others). Source coverage differs between languages.
- **Age groups.** 5–7 (with an adult), 8–10, 11–13, 14+.
- **Languages.** Interface and content in 10 languages (en, ru, de, es, fr, hi, id,
  pt, tr, vi). Depth differs by language; native-speaker review is not complete.
- **Open source.** GPL v3. Source on GitHub. Named author with a public GitHub profile.

## What children learn

- What AI is and is not (not alive, not conscious, not a friend)
- How machine learning works (training on data, not magic)
- Why AI can be wrong, biased, or "hallucinate"
- How to spot AI-generated content (deepfakes, phishing, voice clones)
- When to check with a trusted adult or an independent source

## Frequently asked questions

**Q: What are AI hallucinations — and how do I explain them?**
A: AI hallucinations are confident wrong answers. A language model may cite a non-existent book, invent a fake author, or state a fabricated statistic with complete certainty. For children: 'Imagine a classmate who never admits they don't know — they always make something up. That's how AI works when it's uncertain.' It has not been fully solved: a language model produces plausible text rather than checking facts (survey by Ji et al., ACM Computing Surveys, 2023). Practical rule for children 8+: any AI-provided fact needs verification in at least one independent source.

**Q: What's a good family AI agreement?**
A: Rather than a long document, three commitments cover most households: what stays private (never share a full name plus address, passwords, or photos with a chatbot), when to double-check (any AI-provided fact that matters gets verified against a real source before it's trusted or repeated), and one AI-free habit (for homework: think for five minutes alone first, then explain the AI's answer back in your own words). And one reminder for everyone: AI is a tool, not a friend, no matter how warm it sounds. Make it a short conversation, not a contract, and come back to it now and then — rules whose reasons are understood are followed more willingly than rules that are simply dictated.

**Q: Should kids use AI chatbots?**
A: The question is less 'whether' than 'from what age and how'. UNESCO's 2023 guidance advises an age limit of 13 for AI tools in the classroom; many services also set their own minimum age in their terms — check it. Younger children: only together with an adult. For teenagers a chatbot is fine for looking up a fact and verifying it, or for getting unstuck on homework after a genuine attempt. 'AI companions' — bots that act as a friend — are a separate story: Common Sense Media's study 'Talk, Trust, and Trade-Offs' (2025) describes the risks of exactly such bots for teens. This site deliberately has no chat, no persona and no data collection.

**Q: Is AI appropriate for toddlers and preschoolers (ages 3-5)?**
A: At this age the goal isn't 'using AI' — it's one simple mental model: AI is a machine that follows rules, not a living thing. Preschoolers grasp this through play and comparison ('a robot is like a toy that can answer — it doesn't feel happy or sad'), not through screen time with an actual chatbot. Voice assistants like Alexa or Siri are the most common early exposure; one simple, repeatable rule matters more than conceptual depth at this age: always check with a grown-up.

**Q: From what age should I start explaining AI to my child?**
A: There is no single 'right age' — what matters is what fits each age. Children talk to voice assistants from age 3 and wonder whether they are smart or alive (Druga et al., MIT Media Lab, 2017: children aged 3–10). For preschoolers one simple idea is enough: it is a machine, not a living thing — 'Siri answers, but she doesn't feel anything.' From about 5, patterns, sorting and step-by-step instructions can be explored through play. Younger school children learn to tell AI-made content from real; at 11–13, to understand AI's mistakes and bias; teenagers, to check sources, because generative AI changes what can be trusted online. Short, repeated conversations work better than one big 'AI talk' later on.

**Q: Is Alexa or Siri alive? How do I answer when my toddler asks?**
A: No — and the clearest way to explain it to a 3–5 year old is through comparison: 'Alexa is like a toy that can answer: she has heard a great many words, but she doesn't feel anything, get hungry, or miss you.' Children aged 3–10 playing with voice assistants wonder whether they are smart and who they are (Druga et al., MIT Media Lab, 2017); a short, repeated comparison to a toy — not a lecture — is what actually sticks.

**Q: My child uses AI to write school essays — what's the actual harm?**
A: The harm isn't the tool, it's the skipped step: writing at this age is how kids practice organizing their own thinking, not just producing words. A workable middle ground: draft the ideas and structure alone first, then use AI only to check grammar or suggest phrasing — never to generate the original argument. Even when undetected, the real cost is the lost practice.

**Q: My teenager asked an AI chatbot for medical or legal advice — should I be concerned?**
A: AI chatbots can produce medical- or legal-sounding text with total confidence regardless of whether it's accurate — this is the 'hallucination' problem, and it's how the underlying model works, not occasional carelessness. The rule worth teaching at this age: AI can help you understand a topic or prepare questions, but any actual medical or legal decision needs verification from a real doctor, lawyer, or official source before acting on it.

Full parents' FAQ: https://iamalex-afk.github.io/kids-ai-test/#parent

## Age groups and content

- 5–7, with an adult: an adult reads aloud, the child chooses and tries; yes/no questions, letter-collecting snake
- 8–10: word-collecting snake, 4-option quiz, stories with examples
- 11–13: deepfakes, algorithmic feeds, data privacy, AI bias
- 14+: technical depth, policy, self-assessment

## Technical facts

- Vanilla JS + Canvas API, no frameworks
- Card number = seconds since 2026-07-01 00:00 UTC by the device clock. Its SHA-256 code is a
  fingerprint of the card's own fields, not a signature: it proves neither identity, nor
  uniqueness, nor course completion.
- Works offline after the first full visit (service worker cache); a lesson page
  works offline only if it was opened before

## Site structure

- / (index.html) — English
- /ru.html, /de.html, /es.html, /fr.html, /hi.html, /id.html, /pt.html, /tr.html, /vi.html
- /lessons/<lang>/ — catalog of all lessons by age, per language (en, ru, de, es, fr, hi, id, pt, tr, vi)
- /lessons/<lang>/<age>-<n>.html — one lesson per page; age is 5-7, 8-10, 11-13 or 14-plus.
  The same lessons as on the main page: explanation, example, a check with an explained answer.
